chapter: Later life, World's Fair and Ellington
title: Playing at the duPont pavilion at the World's Fair
summary: Hall tells of playing every fifteen minutes and the plastic bass photograph incident.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Uh-huh, When did you work at the World's Fair and with who?
I worked at duPont at the last World's Fair.
Yeah, the one in '60 --
Both years.
When was it, '69?
No, not that late,
Oh, no, excuse me, '64 and '65, right in there.
Because I remember Shea Stadium opened the second year of the Fair. The Mets came in at the Shea Stadium.
No, the Shea Stadium was already open,
Oh. In '60 --
It was across the road.
Yeah. Anyway, you worked in the duPont Building?
Yeah, chemistry, in chemistry, with --
: With --

-- well, there were various -- there was [NORMAN PARIS] one band, and I'm trying to think of his name. He's dead now. He had the band, but they were three different groups, because the music was continuous from morning until it closed at night.
And -- oh, it was Warren Chiasson. We were working together. And Charlie Simon was doing the rhythms.
: The drummer, yeah.
She was working in. And the other guys were itinerant, more or less, vibes and -- vibes and piano, drums, bass, guitar. Every 15 minutes we were on.
(Laughter.)
Standard tunes.
: Strange schedule.

Oh, wow, that was real weird. They had a laboratory demonstration for all the things that we're using now like Mylar and -- what's the name, Corfam shoes and things like that that they were testing, chemicals that --
: You didn't get much rest period, did you?
No, 15 minutes.
: 15 minutes on and 15 minutes off?
15 minutes on, 15 minutes off. They had a theater where they show a film, and then the crowd from the

theater came into the -- the experimental portion of the room where they stood, and then we played. We played for them to come in, and then we played for the performers when they -- whatever they were doing with pews, and then we played for the crowd to leave.
And then you had 15 minutes.
And then we had 15 minutes off.
Do whatever you had to do.
But there's another crowd waiting to come in,
(Laughter.)
This happened all day long. And the brass, oh, boy, what a tight shift that was. If you did anything wrong, it was reported right away. All of it was.
Funny thing happened to me there. We used the plastic bass, the baby bass. Are you aware of the baby bass?
The Ampeg.
Yeah, the Ampeg.
Yeah, Bill Pemberton used to play one of those.

Yeah. Well, we all had to play that, So this morning I got in. We're supposed to start at 10:00 o'clock. You've got to go up to the fourth floor and change into your uniform, which is a red jacket, bow tie, et cetera, and be back downstairs for the 10:00 o'clock cue.
(Laughter.)

You just get off the subway, You've got to run upstairs, run back, and somebody's there watching you with a stopwatch almost. So I see all these cameras, and there's a cameraman wants to take pictures of me.
Now, I don't know why, because I didn't get a chance to talk to anybody. Time I got back downstairs to make my cues, it was time for me to play. And he photographed me throughout the set.
So when we finished, I questioned him, you know, how come me? And he was taking pictures of the bass that was made by another plastic company than duPont.
(Laughter.)
Somebody heard about it and reported it. So here comes a memo. No pictures. I forget the name of the chemical -- chemical company, but they -- they're the ones that --
Made the plastic for the bass.
-- plastic for the bass.
There was only one bass like that, wasn't there?
Yeah. It was only one bass like that. But duPont didn't do it.
(Laughter.)
Yeah. So they didn't want anyone else.
No, No, We had all kinds of things like that.
(Laughter.)
